subclaims.claim: A thick stone wall ("stone fence") ran parallel to and behind the Twelfth Corps breastworks on Culp's Hill and was held by Confederate troops on the night of 2-3 Jul.
subclaims.why: Williams ("less than 50 yards behind"), Geary ("occupied by a force of the enemy as a protection against attack from the direction of the turnpike"). Distance groups 30-75 yd versus 200 yd are carried by fence-2 (DD-F2-06).

subclaims.claim: The wall was attacked in the early morning of 3 Jul, not at 10:00-11:00: the Union battery shelled the Confederates from 03:45 (Candy), the 1st Maryland PHB attacked the wall about 04:00 (Maulsby), and the 147th Pennsylvania was ordered to charge and carry the wall at 05:00 (Geary), the enemy then abandoning the entire line of the stone wall.
subclaims.why: Three independent reports give 03:45, about 04:00 and 05:00. Pardee's own report (R301 p.846) names an attempt at about 08:00 to turn the right of the works and no wall.

subclaims.claim: The 1st Maryland (Potomac Home Brigade) attacked "a position of the enemy on the right, behind a stone wall" about 04:00 and nearly reached it.
subclaims.why: Maulsby R283 p.806: "the stone wall nearly reached, and bayonets were fixed for a charge over it" before a flanking brigade appeared and the enemy "were distinctly seen fleeing from behind the stone wall".

subclaims.claim: The wall of these reports is the stone wall at the edge of Pardee Field (P-08).
subclaims.why: The OR does not use the name Pardee Field; the 147th PA (Pardee's regiment) is named by Geary and Candy for the charge, and the Comte de Paris (via NPS 1940) puts a stone wall on the small plateau south of Culp's Hill running to the swale toward Rock Creek. NPS names Pardee Field as Abraham Spangler Field 8; no local text says which wall.

subclaims.claim: The Union counterattack at daylight was ordered by Geary under Slocum's orders and opened with artillery at 03:30-04:30.
subclaims.why: Candy 03:45 battery; Geary R293 ("at 3.30 a. m. (early dawn) a simultaneous attack was made by artillery and the infantry"); the printed trigger "Geary's counterattack" is therefore the dawn attack, hours before the 10:00-11:00 window.

subclaims.claim: The last Confederate charge came at 10:25-10:30 (two brigades of Johnson's division, the 1st Maryland Battalion leading) and was repulsed; this was the last charge.

subclaims.claim: Twelfth Corps batteries stood on the hill known as Slocum's headquarters (Powers Hill): Knap's (E, Pennsylvania, six 10-pounders; Lt Atwell), Battery M, 1st New York (four 10-pounders) a quarter mile east of it, and the right section of Battery M under Lt Woodbury on Powers' Hill by the battery's own history.
subclaims.why: Hunt, Muhlenberg and the battery history. The OR calls the hill Slocum's headquarters or Slocum's Hill; "Powers' Hill" is the battery history's name.

subclaims.claim: The Twelfth Corps artillery (placed during the night by Lt Col Best) opened at 04:00 (Slocum), 04:30 (Hunt, Muhlenberg, Ruger) on the morning of 3 Jul; Muhlenberg's two rifle and two 12-pounder batteries (twenty guns) fired fifteen minutes without intermission at 600-800 yards, then at intervals from 05:30 to 10:00.

subclaims.claim: The guns fired because Meade's headquarters moved (printed trigger).

corrected_claim: Cushing's battery (six 3-inch rifles) stood at the Angle behind a pre-existing stone wall and a fence: three limbers blew up at about 08:00 on 3 Jul (Hazard, Hall); by 14:45 all the guns but one had been silenced (Webb); when the assault came three guns were run down to the fence/wall and Cushing was killed there (Webb, Hall, Hazard, Bachelder). "Four of six guns knocked out" is not supported by any text.

subclaims.claim: A stone wall and a fence stood on the Cemetery Ridge line where Webb's brigade and Cushing's battery formed on 2 Jul: Webb put the 69th Pennsylvania "behind a fence a little in advance of the ridge" at 06:30 on 2 Jul with his right on Cushing's battery, and Gibbon had the brigade "partially behind a low stone wall" at about 16:00.
subclaims.why: Existence of the wall and fence before the assault, on the day before it; no OR text describes their construction, so no construction animation is justified (CLAUDE.md, pre-existing features).

subclaims.claim: Three limbers of Cushing's Battery A, 4th US Artillery, exploded when the Confederate guns opened suddenly at about 08:00 on the morning of 3 Jul, with little other loss.
subclaims.why: Hazard dates it "about 8 o'clock"; Hall confirms "three of his limbers were blown up". The printed "(morning)" is now an hour.

subclaims.claim: By 14:45 the Confederate cannonade had "silenced the Rhode Island battery and all the guns but one of Cushing's battery" (Webb); the battery had six 3-inch rifles.
subclaims.why: The printed "four of six guns knocked out" has no source: Webb says all but one of the battery's guns were silenced, not four of six. "Silenced" is not "knocked out" (disabled); no OR text counts the disabled pieces.

subclaims.claim: Four of the six guns were knocked out (printed).
subclaims.why: Contradicted in wording by Webb ("all the guns but one" silenced by 14:45) and by Webb's "Three of Cushing's guns were run down to the fence" afterwards; no text gives four.

subclaims.claim: When the assault came (from 15:00) three of Cushing's guns were run down to the fence/wall with their canister, and Cushing, severely wounded, "pushed his gun to the fence in front" and was killed there.
subclaims.why: Webb p.428, Hall p.438, Hazard p.480, Bachelder. The OR calls the line "the fence" and "the wall" (Webb: "advanced to the wall on the right of the Sixty-ninth"; "the enemy advanced steadily to the fence"; Armistead "passed over the fence").

subclaims.claim: The line the guns were run to had a stone wall with a rail fence in or at it: Hall "the slight cover of the rail fence", Abbott the enemy "behind a rail fence", Webb's "fence" and "stone wall", Smith "protected by a stone wall", Fitzhugh "the stone fence in front of General Webb".
subclaims.why: Several witnesses use "fence" and "wall" for the same line; whether a rail fence ran on top of, in front of or beside the stone wall is not stated. The wall itself shows no damage in any text read.

subclaims.claim: The state changes run from about 08:00 on the morning of 3 Jul (limbers) to the assault at 15:00-15:30 (guns run to the wall, Cushing killed).
subclaims.why: The printed upper bound "about 15:30" is the end of the assault at the Angle; the OR has no clock time for Cushing's death (Webb: "At 3 o'clock the enemy's line of battle left the woods").

corrected_claim: Leister house, 3 Jul: the cannonade from about 13:00 (to about 14:30-15:00) put shells through the yard (staff horses tied to the fence), the steps, the porch supports, the door and the garret; the house was shot through several times and many horses lay dead around it (Captain Meade, Haskell, NPS); when Lydia Leister returned she found 17 dead horses, the hay gone and her fence rails burned, and the surrounding fences damaged (NPS). "All" rails, the hour of the burning, the bedstead, apple and peach trees and the spoiled spring are not supported by any local text.

subclaims.claim: The Leister house was Meade's headquarters from the early hours of 2 Jul; the Army council of war met there on the night of 2 Jul.
subclaims.why: NPS web pages and Handbook 9. The row's from-state "Meade HQ" is supported.

subclaims.claim: During the Confederate cannonade (from about 13:00 on 3 Jul) shells burst in the yard among the staff horses tied to the fence, tore up the steps, carried away the porch supports and passed through the door and the garret; the house was "shot through several times".
subclaims.why: Captain George Meade Jr. (participant, 1913), Haskell (letter of July 1863), NPS (quoting Meade Jr.); the Sentinel's correspondent places the first shells over the "tiny farm house" at about 13:00. Printed "steps and porch supports down", "many shot holes": supported.

subclaims.claim: 17 dead horses lay in the yard (and more in the Taneytown Road) when Lydia Leister returned.
subclaims.why: "17" rests on the NPS statement alone (the number is from her returned-home account / claim); contemporary and later witnesses (Haskell, NY at Gettysburg) confirm many dead horses around the house without a count.

subclaims.claim: Fence rails at the Leister farm had been burned by the time Lydia Leister returned after the battle; the surrounding fences were damaged.
subclaims.why: NPS says "her fence rails had been burned" and, of the photograph, "the house and surrounding fences are all damaged". Neither says "all", who burned them or when; the printed window 13:00-15:00 on 3 Jul and the structures note "Jul 2-3" are not supported (the troops at the house burned wood on any of the three days and after).

subclaims.claim: The hay was gone from the barn (printed "2 tons hay lost").
subclaims.why: NPS: "all the hay was gone from her barn"; the amount (2 tons) is not in any local text.

subclaims.claim: A shell broke a bedstead; apple trees destroyed; a peach tree died; the spring was spoiled.
subclaims.why: Searched bedstead, apple trees, peach tree, spring in all local texts: nothing for the Leister farm (the only peach tree is the living one with a bird's nest at about 13:00 in the Sentinel reprint). The PDF source is the damage claim via Stone Sentinels.

subclaims.claim: The damage fell between about 13:00 and 15:00 on 3 Jul during the cannonade.
subclaims.why: Hunt: opened at about 1 p.m.; Union fire gradually stopped at about 2.30 p.m. and the enemy slackened soon after (end of the shelling 14:30-15:00; Hancock 1 h 45 min, Gibbon two hours, Lee about two hours; C-029 carried by the r03 shard). Applies to the shell damage and the dead horses, not to the rails.

corrected_claim: Emmitsburg Road fences: double post-and-rail (post-and-plank) fences enclosed both sides of the road and stood on the line of the advance on 3 Jul (Peyton, Shepard, Davis; NPS); the attackers had to climb them and crowded at the openings where they had been thrown down (Martin via NPS; Davis). subclaims.claim: Post-and-rail (and post-and-plank) fences stood on the line of the advance on 3 Jul and had to be climbed: Peyton climbed "three high post and rail fences"; Shepard reached "a lane inclosed by two stout post and plank fences" 180-200 yards from the Union works, "a very great obstruction"; Davis met "a strong post and rail fence" and "other fences of a similar character".
subclaims.why: Three Confederate brigade or regiment reports. The "lane inclosed by two fences" is the double fence along a road; Shepard does not name the road; NPS names the Emmitsburg Road (below).

subclaims.claim: Double post-and-rail fences enclosed both sides of the Emmitsburg Road, and the soldiers who reached it had to scale them.
subclaims.why: NPS Record of Treatment vol. I and the Emmitsburg Road Ridge inventory (institutional secondary, Law cl.4: not a primary but a non-lead source), supported by Shepard's "lane inclosed by two fences" and Martin's "parallel fences" (via NPS).

subclaims.claim: The fences slowed the advance and the attackers broke ranks to climb: "large numbers were shot down on account of the crowding at the openings where the fences had been thrown down, and on account of the halt in order to climb the fences" (Martin, 53rd Virginia); Davis: the alignment "became more or less deranged".
subclaims.why: Printed "slowed the charge about 15:30-16:15; attackers broke ranks to climb": supported without the hours. The clock: Webb has the line leaving the woods and crossing the road about 15:00 and Eshleman about 30 minutes after the signal; no text gives 15:30-16:15 for the fences.
